Hair Care

Curly Hair Care

Home / Hair Care / Curly Hair

Curly hair has different needs than straight hair at almost every step of a routine — from how it's washed to how it's dried to how often it's brushed. A lot of common hair advice is written with straight hair in mind, which is part of why curly hair can feel harder to figure out. This guide covers the basics that tend to make the biggest difference.

Moisture First

Curly hair tends to be naturally drier than straight hair because scalp oils travel less easily down the curl pattern — every bend in the hair shaft slows that natural conditioning process. Rich conditioners, leave-ins and periodic deep treatments help offset that, and many curly-hair routines lean more heavily on conditioner than shampoo for this reason.

Reducing Frizz

  • Apply product to soaking-wet hair for better distribution — curls absorb and hold product more evenly when hair is fully saturated.
  • Use a microfiber towel or cotton t-shirt instead of a regular towel, since standard towel fibers rough up the cuticle and increase frizz.
  • Avoid brushing dry curls — detangle with fingers or a wide-tooth comb when wet and conditioned instead.
  • Consider a diffuser attachment if you blow-dry, which distributes airflow more gently across curls than a direct dryer nozzle.

Building a Simple Routine

A workable starting routine is: cleanse with a gentle, sulfate-free shampoo (not necessarily every wash day — many curly routines "co-wash" with conditioner more often than they shampoo), follow with a generous conditioner, apply a leave-in and styling product to soaking-wet hair, and let curls air-dry or diffuse rather than towel-drying roughly. Adjust from there based on how your specific curl pattern and porosity respond.

Sleeping and Protecting Curls

A silk or satin pillowcase (or a loose silk bonnet) causes far less friction overnight than cotton, which helps curls hold their shape and reduces breakage over time. Loosely gathering curls into a "pineapple" — a high, loose ponytail on top of the head — before bed can also help preserve the curl pattern from one day to the next without a full restyle each morning.

Getting a Curl-Friendly Haircut

When you do go in for a cut, ask specifically whether your stylist cuts curly hair dry. Curls shrink significantly once they're fully dry and settled, so a cut done wet can end up shorter or less balanced than intended. A stylist experienced with curls will typically cut (or at least final-shape) the hair dry to see exactly how it falls.

Product Buildup and Clarifying

Curl-friendly styling products — gels, creams, and heavier leave-ins — can build up on the hair over time, especially if you're not shampooing very often. That buildup often shows up as dullness, flatness, or curls that suddenly feel harder to define even though your routine hasn't changed. A monthly clarifying shampoo, used sparingly since it can also strip needed moisture, helps reset the hair before returning to a normal routine.

Different Curl Patterns, Different Needs

Loose waves and tight coils don't behave identically, even though general curly-hair advice often treats them as one category. Looser patterns tend to need lighter products and can often tolerate more frequent washing without drying out, while tighter coil patterns usually need richer products and benefit from stretching techniques — like braiding or twisting sections while damp — to manage shrinkage and encourage more visible length. If general curly-hair advice isn't quite working, looking for guidance specific to your curl pattern is often the next useful step.

See also: Haircuts for Curly Hair.

Patience Is Part of the Process

Curly hair often takes longer to feel "figured out" than straight hair, simply because there are more variables at play. Give any new routine a few weeks before judging it, and adjust one variable at a time.
